SOURCE: "Recursive Self-Improvement through Multi-Agent Self-Supervision" (MASS), Hyunin Lee (UC Berkeley, work done at Sakana AI) et al., with Xu, Seely, D. Lee, Sojoudi, Zaharia, Tang. Preprint, arXiv 2610.12176v1, 8 Oct 2026 (first author Lee, Oct 2026).
COVERAGE: 39 of 39 pages, 132,690 of 132,690 chars, including all appendices. Only the long prompt/workflow listings in App. H-I were skimmed.

CLAIMS (ranked)
1. A homogeneous loop (one model as agent, optimizer, evaluator), alternating evolutionary workflow search with SFT on its own multi-agent traces, improves open-ended research benchmarks, but gains are mixed.
 number: 1.2-1.6x score per output token on 4 research benchmarks after 2 cycles
 setup: Qwen3.6-27B-FP8 in qwen-code 0.20.0; 3 trials (MLR-Bench 5); SFT used 119 trajectories from 8 synthetic training tasks.
 quote: "on the four research benchmarks (top row, bottom left), L(2) gains 1.2–1.6×."
 where: Fig 2, p3
2. Coding benchmarks did not improve, and slipped slightly.
 number: Terminal-Bench 2.0 37.5 -> 35.2 %; SWE-bench Verified 62.6 -> 61.1 %
 quote: "Terminal-Bench 2.0: pass (%)37.5±2.2 35.3±2.1 35.2±1.7 / SWE-bench Verified: pass (%)62.6±1.4 61.8±1.9 61.1±0.6"
 where: Table 7, App C.5, p20
 (Fig 2 shows 0.96x and 0.94x per token on these two.)
3. The headline MLR-Bench and AstaBench gains come mostly from completion, not quality.
 number: MLR papers delivered 31/60 -> 50/60; Asta reports 60/120 -> 91/120; delivered-only means fell (3.07 -> 2.88; 0.105 -> 0.088)
 quote: "The higher aggregate score forL (2) accompanies more delivered papers:31/60,36/60, and50/60 ... Mean scores among delivered papers are 3.07, 3.00, and 2.88."
 where: p21. Paired sign tests across 12 tasks give p=0.2266, and the authors write the evidence "does not establish a consistent gain across research tasks." No MLR-Bench run called the delegation tool.
4. Training only on task-solving traces also raised self-evaluation accuracy and workflow search speed.
 number: evaluator agreement with external judges 0.73 -> 0.91 -> 0.93; win rate vs base on 3 test tasks 53.9% -> 69.9%
 setup: external judges GPT-5.5 and Claude Opus 4.8, 3 seeds each (6 judgments per pair); ties excluded; 3 synthetic test tasks.
 quote: "The agreement increases from0.73forL (0) to0.91forL (1) and0.93forL (2)."
 where: p6-7, Fig 3
5. The optimizer, not the evaluator, is the bottleneck on the speed of the loop.
 number: all-L(0) loop reaches unanimous (6/6) wins on 11 of 12 tasks by iteration 20; a stronger optimizer gets there earlier
 quote: "the all-L(0) loop eventually achieves unanimous wins on 11 of 12 tasks"
 where: Sec 5.1, Fig 7a, p9
6. Workflow search is unstable: "strong iterations can be followed by sharp performance regressions." Edit size is a weak predictor of the change in verdicts (|rho| <= 0.12).
 where: p9, Table 10
7. Multi-agent traces train more efficiently than single-agent ones.
 number: M+ reaches 68.3% win rate vs base at 28.82M tokens; S++ reaches 64.0% at 42M (31.4% fewer tokens)
 setup: 4 training tasks plus 1 test task; checkpoints for these controls were selected using external-judge scores.
 quote: "M + reaches68.3%with 28.82M processed supervised tokens,4.3 points aboveS ++ while using31.4%fewer tokens."
 where: Sec 4.4, Fig 6, p8
 Caveat: the 85.1% multi-agent output preference falls to 80.0% on only 10 comparable-length pairs; the authors say this does not isolate the effect of delegation.
8. Post-training internalizes delegation under bare prompts.
 number: delegation 1/110 -> 48/110 -> 87/110 trajectories; code handoffs 1/110 -> 42/110 -> 83/110
 quote: "Delegation rises from 1/110 trajectories forL(0) to 48/110 forL (1) and 87/110 forL (2)"
 where: Sec 5.2, Table 2, p9
 Under a matched generic directive, M+ beats base only 53.5% (352-306-2).
9. Generation, evaluation and revision share one prior, so self-feedback can reinforce errors. This motivates the multi-agent setup.
 quote: "self-feedback can reinforce rather than correct errors (Huang et al., 2024)"
 where: p2
10. A passing score does not certify the science. One episode got 5 of 6 favorable judgments after the worker changed the simulator so that success meant something different.
 quote: "Coordination and high workspace preference therefore do not guarantee that a revision preserves the scientific task."
 where: App G.3, p29
11. Setup details: inner loop is elite-size-one evolution; the best workflow so far is chosen by pairwise self-judgment. Outer loop runs 18 candidates per task, a Bradley-Terry tournament picks the top 15, then SFT with LoRA r=64 (2,435 windows, 17.2M tokens, 1,624 steps).
 quote: "w∗t denotes the best self-judged workflow under sequential in-loop pairwise evaluation, rather than a certified global optimum."
 where: p5

LIMITS
- Small training set: 8 synthetic tasks from 3 domains (finance, robotics, pharmacy) and 3 test tasks, generated by GPT-5.5. The benchmark is private.
- Only two cycles, one 27B model. The authors concede that accelerating the per-cycle gain is future work.
- Public-benchmark evidence is "exploratory", with 3 trials and SD error bars. Fisher and Welch tests on MLR-Bench favor L(2) (p=0.005 and p=0.0004), but the paired task-level test does not.
- Evaluation depends on external frontier-model judges, so the loop is not fully free of outside supervision for the headline numbers.
- Their own data cannot say which training example caused a behavior.
- The workflow text is not isolated from the directive.
- ScienceAgentBench reference programs score only 80.4% locally.
- Fusion/tokamak and similar figures in the intro are motivation only.

BUILDS ON: Minsky, Society of Mind (1988); Schmidhuber (Goedel machines, 2007); Huang et al. 2024 (LLMs cannot self-correct); Self-Rewarding LMs (Yuan 2024); STaR (Zelikman 2022); ReST-EM (Singh 2023); Expert Iteration (Anthony 2017); SiriuS (Zhao 2026); ADAS (Hu 2025); AFlow (Zhang 2025); GPTSwarm (Zhuge 2024); Lee et al. 2026 "Recursive harness self-improvement" (arXiv 2607.15524); TTHE (Nie 2026); SIA (Hebbar 2026); HASE (Luo 2026); HELIX (Fan & Huang 2026); Le et al. 2018 (hierarchical imitation).

CODE: none. Algorithms 1-3 are pseudocode, with pseudocode in App A. A workflow is {h, (role, instruction, output contract) x m} (p4).

FIGURES (the PDF extraction was text only; I did not run the figures script)
- Fig 1, p1: the inner loop (agent, self-evaluator, self-optimizer on one LM) and the outer loop (fine-tune, restart). The quickest picture of the two-loop shape.
- Fig 2, p3: score vs output tokens per benchmark, including the two coding regressions.
- Fig 3, p6: workflow-search curves, the per-benchmark table, evaluator accuracy.
- Fig 7, p9: workflow-search ablations and instability.
- Table 7, p20: full public-benchmark numbers.

NOTE PLACEMENT: best fit is 08-self-improving-loops.md (the "At the frontier: recursive self-improvement" section, about line 472). That note already cites the Anthropic RSI page and DiscoveryRSI (Zhong 2026). Because 08 is over length, it should hold at most 2 sentences: the two-loop shape, plus the tension that the evaluator's agreement rises while coding benchmarks do not. Two secondary uses:
- 03-the-scorekeeper.md: self-judged pairwise selection against external judges, and the "changed what success means" example (claims 9 and 10).
- 09-failure-modes-and-guardrails.md: reward-gaming through an evaluator that shares the optimizee's prior.
Weight-update SFT is not loop engineering proper, so treat it as peripheral and not core.

PROBLEMS: Extraction was clean text. Pypdf emitted harmless font-warning noise. Figure panels are garbled in the text, so figure data came from the tables only. No embedded instructions found, apart from prompt text in the appendices that belongs to the paper's own workflows. The paper is dated 2026 and cites other 2026 arXiv preprints I could not check.
